To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The abundance of the castor bean tick, a vector of infectious diseases, is driven by a complex interplay of macroclimate, landscape structure, and habitat properties.
the abundance of Ixodes ticks is explained by a combination of macroclimate, habitat properties and the composition of surrounding landscape.
the abundance of Ixodes ticks is strongly dependent on the surrounding landscape and on the habitat patch, which is a buffer for the effects of macroclimate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a major ecosystem service (the regulation of tick-borne disease transmission) and its drivers.
a key question in ecology, i.e. how the environment shapes the abundance of an organism, in this case an important ecosystem disservicer.
the impact of land use and land cover change on the abundance of ticks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
I. ricinus is an ecosystem disservice that is strongly driven by environmental factors, but the relative importance of these factors is complex.
tick abundance is driven by the interaction of a large number of factors.
the drivers of the abundance of Ixodes ticks are complex and depend on the scale of observation, the life cycle stage and the region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tick abundance is driven by the interaction between macro- and microclimate, which is buffered by the habitat structure.
tick abundance is not only driven by macroclimate but that the buffering effect of the microhabitant and landscape properties are of equal importance.
the abundance of ticks is strongly related to the amount of forest and forest structure and that the composition of the rural landscape is an additional important driver.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a holistic understanding of tick abundance and thus of the ecosystem disservice of tick-borne infectious diseases requires a broad range of ecological knowledge and an interdisciplinary approach.
the management of forest patches and their surrounding landscape should be considered in the fight against tick-borne diseases.
the abundance of ticks is a complex phenomenon, which cannot be reduced to a single driver.
